question: A 45-year-old woman on long-term metoclopramide for gastroparesis develops repetitive, involuntary, stereotyped jaw chewing movements and tongue protrusion that persist even after the drug is discontinued. Which drug-induced movement disorder does this represent?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Acute dystonia occurs within hours to days of starting a dopamine antagonist and is characterised by sustained muscle contractions (e.g., oculogyric crisis, torticollis). It is not stereotyped chewing movements, and it resolves rapidly after stopping the drug.

Correct. Tardive dyskinesia (TD) is caused by long-term dopamine receptor blockade (months to years) and classically manifests as oro-buccal-lingual stereotypies — repetitive chewing, lip smacking, tongue protrusion. Crucially, TD often persists or worsens after drug withdrawal (reflecting receptor hypersensitivity), distinguishing it from acute drug-induced parkinsonism.

Incorrect. Drug-induced parkinsonism mimics idiopathic PD with bradykinesia, rigidity, and tremor — not stereotyped oro-buccal movements. It typically resolves within weeks to months of stopping the offending drug.

Incorrect. NMS is a life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction characterised by hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability, and altered consciousness — not stereotyped orofacial dyskinesia. It requires immediate drug cessation and intensive supportive care.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the spectrum of drug-induced movement disorders: acute dystonia (hours–days, painful, responds to anticholinergics), drug-induced parkinsonism (weeks–months, resolves on stopping), tardive dyskinesia (months–years, often irreversible, oro-buccal stereotypies), akathisia (subjective restlessness), and NMS (life-threatening emergency).

Excellent. Tardive dyskinesia is a critical drug-induced movement disorder to recognise — it affects millions on dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) and can be irreversible. Valbenazine and deutetrabenazine are now approved treatments.
